clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder characterised by microphthalmia or anophthalmia, often asymmetrical, associated with a range of extraocular malformations
Caused by variants in BCOR, a transcriptional corepressor important in early eye, skeletal, cardiac and dental development
Extraocular features include skeletal anomalies (digital and limb malformations), dental abnormalities, cardiac and urogenital defects and variable developmental delay
As an X-linked condition, affected males show the full phenotype while carrier females are typically mildly or not affected, though minor dental or ocular signs may occur
The ocular malformation is the most consistent feature and frequently causes significant visual impairment
BCOR variants also underlie oculofaciocardiodental syndrome in females, indicating a related allelic spectrum
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with ophthalmological care, dental and orthopaedic input and developmental support
reference.pathophysiology: Lenz microphthalmia syndrome is caused by variants in the X-linked gene BCOR, which encodes a corepressor that partners with transcription factors to regulate gene expression during development. BCOR is required for the coordinated formation of the eye, skeleton, heart, teeth and urogenital tract, so its disruption produces microphthalmia or anophthalmia together with a spectrum of extraocular malformations including limb and digital anomalies and dental defects. The X-linked inheritance explains the sex difference, with hemizygous males fully affected and heterozygous carrier females usually mildly affected or unaffected. Allelic variants in BCOR give rise to the related oculofaciocardiodental syndrome, reflecting the gene's broad developmental role.
additionalDifferentials: Anophthalmia-microphthalmia from other genetic causes (e.g. SOX2, OTX2)
additionalInvestigations: Detailed ophthalmological examination and orbital imaging to characterise microphthalmia or anophthalmia
Skeletal survey to define digital and limb anomalies
Renal tract imaging for urogenital anomalies
BCOR molecular genetic testing with X-linked segregation analysis
redFlags: Bilateral severe microphthalmia or anophthalmia with profound visual impairment requiring early support
Features suggesting a broader syndromic diagnosis needing urgent evaluation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of the ocular and systemic malformations; visual outcome is often poor because of the microphthalmia, while overall prognosis and development vary with the associated cardiac, renal and neurodevelopmental involvement.
pitfalls: Attributing isolated microphthalmia to a single cause without considering the broader BCOR spectrum and X-linked inheritance
Overlooking extraocular skeletal, cardiac and renal anomalies that require dedicated assessment
Failing to identify mildly affected carrier females and the allelic oculofaciocardiodental phenotype when counselling
Neglecting early developmental and visual support for affected children
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: There is no specific drug therapy; management focuses on the ocular malformation and the associated systemic anomalies
Manage microphthalmia or anophthalmia with orbital conformers or expanders and prosthetics to promote orbital growth, alongside low-vision aids and visual rehabilitation
Assess and treat associated cardiac defects and urogenital anomalies, with surgical correction where indicated
Provide developmental support, dental care and management of skeletal and digital anomalies
Monitor cardiac and renal function and developmental progress through multidisciplinary follow-up
Offer genetic counselling for this X-linked BCOR condition, including carrier assessment of female relatives and family segregation analysis
